title: Service-tier aware capacity-capping experiments
content:
Summary:

These are field notes from an experiment series exploring a service-tier-aware capacity capping heuristic for our continuous batching scheduler. Goal: reduce 95/99/99.9th tail latency regressions for premium (gold) tenants without disproportionately increasing e2e latency for non-premium (standard) workloads, and without materially degrading throughput on high-concurrency nodes.

Motivation / Problem Statement:
- In mixed-tenant clusters we observed that occasional microbursts from low-priority traffic can inflate batch formation latency for high-priority requests. Existing urgency-weighted batching reduced some impact but still allowed capacity-filling behavior where a long-running large batch (mostly low-priority) delayed flush decisions and increased tail latency for gold requests.
- We need a lightweight heuristic that: (a) enforces soft capacity for non-premium traffic per slot, (b) lets premium requests preempt filling when close to configured SLOs, and (c) gracefully scales back during steady-state so we don't waste GPU throughput.

Hypotheses:
1) Introducing a per-slot capacity cap for standard-tier requests (cap percentage of slot tokens) will reduce premium-tier tail latency at p99 by at least 20% during mixed bursts, with <5% increase in standard-tier median latency.
2) A decay mechanism that increments the cap back to default over a 30s moving window will avoid throughput loss during sustained high standard traffic.
3) Combining cap-capping with timeout-adaptive flush (shorter timeouts when premium queue age > threshold) gives better p99 tradeoffs than either alone.

Experiment design:
- Scheduler baseline: current continuous-batch scheduler with urgency weights and global batch token limit = 4096.
- New control knobs introduced for experiments:
  * cap_pct_standard (0..100) - max percent of slot tokens consumable by standard requests when premium queue non-empty.
  * decay_window_secs - seconds over which cap_pct increments back to 100 after premium queue empties.
  * premium_age_threshold_ms - age of premium requests in queue that triggers aggressive flushing (shorten per-slot timeout by factor).
- Matrix: 3 x 3 x 3 grid
  * cap_pct_standard = [40, 60, 80]
  * decay_window_secs = [10, 30, 120]
  * premium_age_threshold_ms = [15, 50, 200]
- Workloads: synthetic mixture that approximates observed production ratios
  * Node type A (mixed): 30% premium, 70% standard; arrival pattern: baseline Poisson + 30s microburst every 120s of heavy standard traffic
  * Node type B (premium-heavy): 70% premium, 30% standard; steady Poisson
  * Sequence lengths: short (average 20 tokens) for interactive, long (average 600 tokens) for batchy background ops. We mix 80/20 short/long.
- Duration: 2 hours per configuration to capture several microbursts; replicate 3 runs for variance.
- Metrics collected (per-tenant tier): p50, p95, p99, p99.9 latency (ms), throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, average batch size (tokens and requests), fairness index (Jain's index computed on latency improvement relative to baseline). Also track number of preemptive flushes and wasted batch slots (slots with >50% unused tokens when flushed).

Quick implementation notes:
- Added lightweight accounting in the slot allocator: track tokens_occupied_by_standard and tokens_occupied_total. On slot fill, if tokens_occupied_by_standard / slot_capacity > cap_pct_standard apply conservative acceptance (throttle standard adds) unless premium queue non-empty and premium_age > premium_age_threshold_ms.
- Decay implemented as small additive step every second after premium queue empty: cap_pct_standard += (100 - cap_pct_standard) * (1 / decay_window_secs)

Results (high level):
- Best-config (tradeoff) observed: cap_pct_standard=60, decay_window_secs=30, premium_age_threshold_ms=50.
  * Premium p99 reduced by ~28% during mixed bursts compared to baseline (e.g., 320ms -> 230ms).
  * Premium p99.9 improved by ~35%.
  * Standard median latency increased by ~3-6% (acceptable), p95 increased by ~8-12% (within SLO for standard).
  * Throughput (tokens/sec) across node types decreased by ~2-4% in short-run bursts but recovered as decay reopened capacity.
- Aggressive cap (40%) solved premium tail more but caused higher standard p95 increases and visible throughput loss for long sequences (25% throughput drop in worst-case microburst). Decay window mitigated some but not enough.
- Loose cap (80%) gave small premium benefits only; not worth complexity.
- Combining cap with premium_age_threshold adaptive timeout had additive effect: when premium_age_threshold_ms=50, we saw an additional ~10% improvement on p99 over cap-only config. Mechanism: timely short flush allowed premium requests to break out of low-priority-filled slots.

Observed side-effects and edge-cases:
- Cold start: when a node receives bursty standard traffic before any premium traffic, cap limits can underutilize GPU until decay completes. To avoid this we clamp cap_pct_standard to min( configured, observed_standard_fraction * 1.2 ) in the first 30s of node life — simple bootstrap heuristic.
- Long-running single-request sequences (600+ tokens) from standard tenants could block preemption if they were already inside an execution batch; we documented a minor change to prefer inserting premium requests into the front of batch queues when feasible to reduce blocking. This required careful KV-cache consistency checks.
- Observability: added batch-level labels (slot_id, tokens_by_tier, flush_reason) so we can reconstruct preemptive vs timeout-driven flushes in traces. This was crucial to explain p99 improvements.

Representative numbers (example run):
- Baseline mixed node during burst:
  * Premium p99: 320ms, p99.9: 620ms
  * Standard p95: 220ms, p99: 430ms
- Best-config run:
  * Premium p99: 230ms, p99.9: 410ms
  * Standard p95: 240ms, p99: 480ms
  * Avg batch size (tokens): baseline 1830 -> best-config 1600 during burst windows (more smaller batches for premium).

Interpretation / takeaways:
- A modest per-slot cap for low-priority traffic (around 60%) combined with a ~30s decay window produces the best balance for our mixed-tenant patterns. It prevents slots from being dominated by background traffic during microbursts while allowing recovery for sustained backgrounds.
- Adaptive flush (shortening timeouts when premium age rises) is an easy, cheap win when combined with capping — it helps premium requests escape quickly from slow-filling slots.
- The solution must be conservative in the first 30s of node lifetime to avoid throughput loss during ramp-up.

Operational recommendations:
1) Ship cap_pct_standard=60 default with decay_window_secs=30 and premium_age_threshold_ms=50 as an opt-in feature flag for a subset of clusters (canary 5% nodes) and monitor: premium p99, standard p95, GPU utilization, wasted_slots.
2) Add circuit-breaker: if cluster-wide throughput drops >10% or standard p95 increase >30% on canaries, roll back.
3) Rollouts: canary -> 20% -> 100% over 2 weeks with automatic halt conditions.
4) Instrumentation: require per-slot labels and a Grafana dashboard showing per-tier latency quantiles, tokens_by_tier heatmap, and preemptive_flush_count.
5) Spike tests: add continuous chaos microbursts in staging for 48h to validate decay dynamics.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Would tier-aware caps per-model (not just per-tenant tier) yield better efficiency for models with widely different seq-length profiles? (Next experiment: per-model cap adjustments).
- How does this interact with KV-cache locality and p95 for long-context completions? Need targeted replay with cached vs uncached paths.
- Could we learn cap_pct dynamically using a short-horizon RL controller instead of static decay? Keep low priority on complexity unless needed.

Notes for implementation PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runner/pull/412):
- Keep patch small: core change is in slot_allocator.go with opt-in config. Add metrics: slot_capacity_by_tier, cap_pct_effective, decay_state_seconds.
- Added unit tests around slot fill under cap and integration harness replay that mirrors microburst pattern.

Appendix: quick experiment commands
- run local replay harness: ./tools/replay --profile mixed-burst.json --duration 7200 --cfg experiments/cap60-decay30-age50.yaml
- extract batch traces for slot-id 12345: curl -s "http://trace-api.local/trace?slot_id=12345" | jq .

Concluding remark:
This approach is promising — modest complexity and observable benefits for premium tail latency with acceptable tradeoffs. Recommend a small canary rollout and additional per-model experiments before global enabling.

End of notes.
